If a patient has only one mutation in the isoniazid (INH) resistance genes (either inhA or katG, but not both) and is susceptible to fluoroquinolones (FLQ) and injectable agents, the short-course treatment regimen should be continued. If the line probe assay (LPA) results are inconclusive, a repeat specimen should be sent, and the short-course regimen should still be continued. However, if there is no clinical improvement, switching to a long-course regimen should be considered, and hospitalization may be necessary. 2. The South African TB Program's 2017 eligibility criteria for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) included patients with either an inhA or katG mutation (but not both) and susceptibility to FLQ and injectable agents. These criteria were adapted from slides provided by the South African National TB Program (NTP) and aligned with the WHO's consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment. 3. For children under 12 years of age, particularly younger children with confirmed or presumed rifampicin-resistant (RR) or MDR-TB, the short-course regimen may be considered. In cases where a clinician is uncertain about a patient's eligibility for the short-course regimen, the older South African exclusion criteria from 2017 should be referenced. 4. The composition of the modified standardized treatment regimen for MDR-TB in South Africa (2019) includes linezolid (LZD) and bedaquiline (BDQ). This regimen was adapted from the South African NTP and aligns with the WHO's 2022 guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment. 5. Delamanid is the preferred replacement for injectable agents in the short-course regimen for certain age groups. If high-dose isoniazid (Hh) is extended to six months, and second-line LPA or phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) results are unavailable or uninterpretable, the modified standardized regimen should still include LZD and BDQ. 6. The WHO's 2021 individual patient dataset (IPD) eligibility criteria for MDR/RR-TB include data from clinical trials or programmatic cohorts with at least 25 patients who completed treatment and had an assigned end-of-treatment outcome. Patients must have bacteriologically confirmed MDR/RR-TB, with resistance to rifampicin confirmed by phenotypic or genotypic DST within 365 days prior to treatment initiation. 7. The South African 2019 regimen (SA new) was compared to the WHO's long-course regimen (WHO long) in terms of treatment success, failure, and adverse events. The SA new regimen showed a 10% reduction in treatment success, a 71% reduction in treatment failure, a 38% increase in mortality, and a 33% increase in loss to follow-up compared to the WHO long regimen. There was no significant difference in the occurrence of severe adverse events (Grade 3 or above). 8. Subgroup analyses revealed lower treatment success rates across all subgroups for the SA new regimen compared to the WHO long regimen. The reduction in success was particularly pronounced in patients with prior TB, HIV-negative status, smear-negative disease, age ≥15 years, and pulmonary TB. 9. Sensitivity analyses of the WHO IPD 2021 dataset highlighted significant heterogeneity in treatment outcomes across countries. Larger sites in the WHO long dataset, such as India and European regions, had higher success rates than South Africa. This heterogeneity and unmeasured confounding emphasize the importance of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) over observational datasets for guiding treatment decisions. 10. The NExT trial, conducted in South Africa, evaluated the effectiveness of a 6-month all-oral regimen for MDR/RR-TB. The trial used block randomization and included patients aged 18 or older with newly diagnosed pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance confirmed by at least two susceptibility tests. Exclusion criteria included prior MDR-TB treatment, resistance to fluoroquinolones or second-line injectables, and specific medical conditions or medications. 11. The intervention regimen in the NExT trial consisted of five drugs (BDQ, LZD, levofloxacin [LFX], and two Group B or C drugs selected based on genotypic testing). The comparator regimens varied over time, initially including an 18-20 month injectable-based regimen and later a 9-11 month oral regimen. 12. The primary outcome of the NExT trial was the proportion of patients achieving a favorable outcome (cured or treatment completed) without any events defining an unfavorable outcome. The trial demonstrated the feasibility of shorter, all-oral regimens for MDR/RR-TB in community settings.
